title: Helping people in Nepal cope with flood trauma and preparing new early warning systems - People in Need
description: Helping people in Nepal cope with flood trauma and preparing new early warning systems  People in Need
publisher.title: People in Need
full_article:
Difficult access, aid reaching hundreds of people

“Access to the area is still very complicated. Of the 133 kilometres between Kathmandu and Kalikasthan, 90 kilometres run along unpaved roads through difficult terrain. A journey that took around four hours before the disaster now takes twice as long. And some areas can only be reached by air,” says Marek Štys, head of our humanitarian programmes.

“Despite these difficult conditions, we have managed to get material humanitarian aid – food, hygiene supplies, and so-called dignity kits, including underwear – to more than a thousand people. We are also coordinating warehouse management, stock records, and subsequent distribution with local authorities and offices,” adds Marek Štys.

Donate to SOS Nepal

We are also helping local authorities run emergency accommodation centres. “We are keeping the whole centre running, including the kitchen. 51 adults and 12 children are currently staying here,” says Ransubba Gurung from our team, describing how one of the evacuation centres in Rasuwa district operates. “We make sure local people get nutritious, balanced meals. They have four meals a day here, from dal bhat to eggs, cottage cheese, or fresh vegetables,” she adds.

Pomáháme s provozem komunitních kuchyní. (© PIN Nepal)

We are also putting various safety measures in place here to protect the privacy and dignity of people who lost their homes as a result of the disaster.

Coping with trauma and psychosocial support

We have two specialised mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) workers on the ground.

They identified a need for psychological first aid and psychoeducation, not only among residents affected by the disaster but also among frontline workers – rescuers and medical staff, as well as authority and hospital personnel.

This support is now being provided through field visits to people's homes. At the same time, preparations are under way for children's safe return to the classroom, which requires systematic psychosocial care focused on helping them process their experiences of trauma.

How can we prevent further disasters? Early warning systems can help

Our staff are also working with Nepalese authorities, including the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, providing technical support and sharing our experience with early warning systems (EWS). Together, in response to the August floods, we are assessing how the warning systems performed and we are identifying weaknesses and lessons for future improvements.

The aim is to better understand local conditions, monitor how threats develop, identify populations at risk, and determine how much time is available for preventive measures.

The result will be a practical plan covering suitable technologies, the investment required, and clearly defined institutional roles, so that people in the most at-risk areas are protected.

We have years of experience with early warning systems

People in Need has many years of experience with early warning systems (EWS), not only in Nepal but also in Cambodia, Laos, the Philippines, Armenia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In 2025 alone, we protected 1.7 million people in this way.

Thanks to rapid warnings, people are able to protect their lives, property, and livelihoods. Warnings reach them through a range of channels: automated voice calls, SMS, sirens, sign-language video recordings, or community groups on WhatsApp.

Assesing the sites for future early warning systems. (© Sajana Shrestha)

People across the Czech Republic have donated more than CZK 41 million to the SOS Nepal appeal

The solidarity shown by the Czech public has been truly extraordinary. Immediately after the disaster, we released CZK 1 million from our Club of Friends, which allowed us to fund immediate aid before further resources became available.

At the same time, we launched the SOS Nepal appeal, to which people have so far contributed a total of CZK 41.2 million. The appeal remains open.

Next up: insulating shelters and winter supplies

Over the coming months, we will continue providing psychosocial support and plan to launch leisure and educational activities for children.

As winter approaches, we will provide insulated shelters and winter supplies for 1,000 households, and set up temporary latrines, drainage, and water points for a further 100 households.

We will also provide financial assistance to the most vulnerable families and residents, including through “cash for work” programmes, to support their independence and their own livelihood opportunities, and to help contribute to the country's recovery.

title: Nepal Cannot Stop the Floods. It Can Stop Them From Becoming Disasters. - Time Magazine
description: Nepal Cannot Stop the Floods. It Can Stop Them From Becoming Disasters.  Time Magazine
publisher.title: Time Magazine
full_article: Such a transition would not be easy for Nepal. Its infrastructure, businesses and reputation are all geared toward cheap mass tourism. Bhutan’s high-value tourism model benefits from a rarity value: foreign tourists with the exception of Indians have never had easy access to the country. Costa Rica has protected more than a quarter of its landmass in national parks, creating thousands of square miles of protected wilderness for tourists to visit. Other established mass-market destinations, like Thailand, are attempting a similar transition. Nepal could do so, too, but the shift would reduce exposure to disasters only if high-end hotels were built out of harm’s way and the infrastructure supporting them were made resilient.

title: Nepal’s Oscar Contender ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Rallies Flood Relief Efforts at Toronto and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) - Variety

full_article:
Nepal‘s Academy Awards entry “Elephants in the Fog” is the sole Nepali film at the Toronto Film Festival, where director Abinash Bikram Shah has turned the film’s international visibility toward the floods devastating communities back home – among them people directly connected to the production.

Lead actress Puspa Thing Lama is from Nuwakot district, one of the worst-affected areas. Co-producer Prachanda Man Singh Shrestha, also from Nuwakot, has lost his home. “There is something difficult about watching a film travel internationally while people close to it are dealing with the loss of homes and livelihoods,” Shah tells Variety .

The production has already held a fundraising screening in Kathmandu, channeling the proceeds to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund, and has worked with the Zonta Club and Rotary Clubs on support for children caught in the Bhotekoshi flooding. Despite that, “Elephants in the Fog” has carried into its second week since opening Sept. 4, taking in some NPR69 lakh ($45,000) in its first seven days. “But the conversations after screenings have meant just as much to us as the box office,” Shah says.

At the center of the film is Pirati, matriarch of a Kinnar community in a forested Nepalese village, played by first-time screen actress Puspa Thing Lama, who has spent decades as an LGBTIQA+ rights advocate. “She is not simply a representative of a ‘third gender’ community. She is a mother and a leader, with authority, affection, fears and contradictions,” Shah says.

Lama traveled to Cannes when the film took the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize and is now in Toronto. “There is something powerful about seeing someone who has spent decades working to make her community visible now occupying these spaces in her own right, not as a subject being discussed, but as an artist whose performance is being recognized,” Shah says. The Asia Pacific Screen Awards have nominated her for best performance; the film also picked up nods for best film and best director.

“I was drawn to the Kinnar community because of the richness and complexity of the community beyond the marginalization,” he says. The relationships between the women gradually became the film’s core – a story about mothers and daughters, and about people creating family when the structures around them have rejected them.

Sales company Best Friend Forever has closed deals across 14 territories. New agreements place the film with MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia, the Film Development Council of the Philippines and Silk Route for inflight. Those join previously announced deals with Arizona Distribution and Les Valseurs Distribution in France, missingFILMs in Germany and Austria, Imovision in Brazil and The Tea Folks Films for domestic Nepal distribution. A pan-Latin America deal is expected shortly; North American rights are in advanced negotiations.

“The film has traveled much further than we ever expected, but its meaning remains rooted in the place where it began,” Shah says.

title: Verified: Philippines Flood Rescue Video Falsely Linked to Nepal Floods - News Mobile
description: Verified: Philippines Flood Rescue Video Falsely Linked to Nepal Floods  News Mobile
publisher.title: News Mobile
full_article:
A video showing two young women holding on to each other amid a strong current is being widely shared on social media with the claim that it shows a mother and her only daughter being swept away and killed during the devastating floods in Nepal.

A Facebook user posted the viral post with the following caption:

इकलौती बेटी के साथ माँ बाढ़ में फँस गई,देखने वाले वीडियो बनाते रहे लेकिन अंत में बाढ़ की जीत हुई।नेपाल बाढ़ के बाद यह सबसे दर्दनाक वीडियो है।

ENGLISH: A mother got trapped in the flood along with her only daughter, onlookers kept making videos but in the end the flood won. This is the most painful video after the Nepal flood.

You can check the post here .

NM VERIFIED

NewsMobile investigated the viral post and found the claims to be false.

To investigate the viral claim, we conducted a reverse image search using keyframes from the video. The search led us to a report published by Cebu Daily News on September 9, 2025, which featured visuals matching those seen in the viral clip.

According to the report, the incident occurred in Barangay Balogo, Guihulngan City, Negros Oriental, Philippines, on September 4, 2025. Two sisters returning home from school became trapped in the strong current of the Kanslakan River after heavy rainfall caused the river to suddenly swell.

The sisters were swept away by the current but managed to grab onto the roots of a tree. Local residents subsequently came to their aid and rescued them safely.

We also found a report by GMA Regional TV dated September 8, 2025, which corroborated these details. It stated that two female students returning from school in Barangay Balogo were caught in a flash flood. The girls managed to hold onto tree roots before locals rescued them from the raging waters.

Further corroboration came from a Must Share News report published on September 11, 2025. According to the report, the two students were swept away while crossing a river in Guihulngan. The video showed them holding onto each other as they struggled against the strong current. They eventually managed to grab onto a tree root and were rescued by local residents.

title: Durango nonprofit raises funds for Nepal-Tibet flood victims - Durango Herald
description: Durango nonprofit raises funds for Nepal-Tibet flood victims  Durango Herald
publisher.title: Durango Herald
full_article:
The Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation was able to provide emergency donations and relief to the village of Timure, Nepal, on the first day of the flooding. The helicopter was able to retrieve and rescue a grandmother and her granddaughter. (Courtesy of the Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation)

A Durango nonprofit with ties to Nepal is raising money for victims of the Nepal-Tibet floods in the small town of Timure, Nepal.

Triggered by a glacial collapse in the Himalayas, floodwaters, debris and rock ripped through towns near the Nepal-Tibet border, wiping away homes, schools, cars and buses. The floods have left an estimated 1,300 people dead and another 5,000 missing so far. The Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation is hosting an all-you-can-eat buffet fundraiser at the Himalayan Kitchen on Monday, Sept. 21, to raise money for people in Timure, Nepal, affected by the floods.

The Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation was founded by Karma Bhotia and his wife, Kumari Bhotia. They both grew up in a small rural farm town in northeastern Nepal called Chyamtang. The couple eventually immigrated to the United States and later opened the Himalayan Kitchen in Durango in 2007. The foundation has built a new school and daycare center in Chyamtang and also provided aid and relief during the 2015 earthquake in Nepal that killed almost 9,000 people.

The foundation is taking a similar approach to its aid as it did to the 2015 earthquake.

“They want to provide items to help the families rebuild their lives through whatever items they need, whether that’s actually funding to help them rebuild their home or to furnish their homes,” said Julie Korb, the foundation’s lead fundraising and event coordinator.

In 2015, the foundation helped build 64 temporary homes, Karma Bhotia said. The materials for the homes could then be repurposed during the construction of permanent residences, Bhotia explained.

“We would like to do the same like that this time also. We just don’t want to waste money to give a bag of rice, sugar or whatever. We would like them to establish their life long-term, permanently,” Bhotia said.

The foundation doesn’t want to waste resources on already distributed items, Bhotia said, so its taking time to figure out who needs what. Figuring that out is eased by the foundation’s Kathmandu board. The foundation operates out of Durango and Kathmandu, and the board president in the Nepal capital has connections to Timure.

Because the foundation has boots on the ground in Nepal, it’s already working in Timure, Bhotia said. When the floods first hit, the foundation was able to provide emergency relief and use a helicopter to evacuate a grandmother and her granddaughter from the area.

Bhotia said the foundation is leveraging its board connection to Timure to wait and see who did not receive aid and ensure the foundation can help them.

The Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation has a board in Kathmandu, Nepal, with connections to the small town of Timure, Nepal. The foundation was able to hire a helicopter to deliver emergency donations on the first day of the flood and rescue the grandmother and granddaughter pictured. (Courtesy of Karma and Jyamu Bhotia Foundation)

“Many people have no connection to government or maybe are not capable to request to get help from others, and we would like to find those people who did not reach out or who did not get help and would like to directly support them,” Bhotia said.

In the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake, the foundation worked with families that also had not received help, whether it was from the government or other nonprofit organizations, Korb said.

But a similar philanthropic approach doesn’t mean the two events were all that similar. Bhotia described the flood as “the worst natural disaster” in Nepal’s history. In addition to a massive death toll and missing persons, the people who survived “lost everything” and “have no idea how to rebuild or relocate,” Bhotia said. The flood was different from the earthquake because everything was washed out; with the earthquake, there were still remnants, Bhotia added.

The foundation is hosting the fundraiser between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Monday, Sept. 21, at the Himalayan Kitchen. The kitchen is normally closed Mondays but will be open for the event. The foundation is asking for a minimum $30 donation for the buffet. For those who can’t make the lunch, an online donation option is available, or donations can be dropped off at the restaurant in cash or check form. Tax donation receipts are available for both online and in-person donations, Korb said.

The Himalayan Kitchen is normally closed on Mondays but will be open with additional seating for the buffet fundraiser on Sept. 21. The buffet and fundraiser is open from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and donors or guests are welcome throughout.

Roughly 99% of donations will go directly to the flood victims because the foundation is entirely volunteer-based, so there are no additional administrative fees to consider, Bhotia and Korb said.

“I feel like it’s kind of a win-win because a lot of times fundraisers are just asking for money, but here you’re getting to have a meal and share some time with other individuals that want to help support this cause, and then you’re able to help these families in the small rural village in Nepal to start their way to recovery,” Korb said.

title: Nepal floods leave thousands homeless as climate finance lags - The New Arab
description: Nepal floods leave thousands homeless as climate finance lags  The New Arab
publisher.title: The New Arab
full_article:
Sarita Pyakurel was working in her fields on the morning of 26 August when she received a call from her nephew, who told her that a flood was coming and that she should return home.

The 48-year-old farmer had seen floods before and didn’t think much of it, assuming that even if the Trishuli River rose, the water would only reach the fields.

She was making her way back to her home in Nuwakot, which lay about 500m from the river, when she saw a torrent of water sweep the local bridge away.

Shocked and in a daze, she rushed the other way up the hill and into a nearby forest.

"We could never have imagined a flood like this," she told The New Arab . "Everyone thought it wouldn’t be very big."

On 26 August, a glacial flood that began up in the Himalayas tore through villages and towns along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in central Nepal, causing widespread devastation. As of 15 September, more than 1,395 people have died, and another 5,130 are still missing, according to Nepali authorities.

People cross the Bhotekoshi River using a tuin in Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal, on September 7, 2026, after a bridge was swept away, disrupting local transportation [Getty]

Sarita had lived in her Nuwakot home for 34 years. She was unable to salvage anything; all she could do was watch as everything was washed away before her eyes.

"We worked for years to build our house," she said, "and it was destroyed within seconds."

The land she once knew so well had turned into a muddy, silty swamp.

Now she can no longer recognise her village, unable to point out where her house, farm, pasture, or neighbourhood used to be.

Her two sisters-in-law, aged 55 and 57, and her 20-year-old nephew were among those swept away. They are still missing.

Sarita told The New Arab she is now staying in a shelter run by her village's rural municipality, where she sleeps in a room shared with 20 others.

"We have nowhere else to go," she said, adding that she wishes the government had provided better accommodation.

<!--/*--><![CDATA[/* ><!--*/ /*--><!]]>*/



A 'climate-driven disaster'

"[River] Bhotekoshi’s devastating floods, which claimed lives and destroyed homes, are a climate-driven disaster,” Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division under Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, told The New Arab .

"While Nepal’s contribution to global carbon emissions is negligible, we are bearing the consequences of emissions from wealthy, industrialised nations. In that sense, we are victims of others’ actions, not our own."

According to glaciologist Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, global warming is heating the Himalayas faster than most regions, accelerating glacier melt and raising the risk of more frequent and severe glacial lake outburst floods and other ice-related disasters.

Between 1990 and 2020, glaciers in the Himalayas and the nearby Hindu Kush range contracted in area by approximately 12%, contributing to a total ice-thickness loss of about 24 meters since 1974, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Researchers who reviewed 493 floods caused by bursting glacial lakes up to 2024 found that the risk of these outbursts is exacerbated by climate change.

They found that the number of glacial lake outburst floods has jumped fivefold since 1950, from an average of 7 per decade to 38, and flagged 407 glacial lakes as potentially dangerous and at risk of bursting.

Related The families still searching after Nepal's deadly flood Nepal Society Live Story Pratik Ghimire

A disaster-prone country

Nepal is no stranger to climate catastrophe.

In April 2015, a 7.8-magnitude earthquake triggered an ice-and-rock avalanche that buried Langtang village, killing around 300 people.

A decade later, on 8 July 2025, the bursting of a temporary glacial lake in Tibet unleashed a surge of water down the Lhende Khola River, killing at least nine people and sweeping away the Miteri Bridge on the Nepal–China border.

Less than a month later, on 30 July, the Bhotekoshi River flooded, damaging roads and other infrastructure along the same corridor.

Initial assessments showed that the latest flood had damaged 7,570 private homes, 48 government buildings, 18 schools, and seven health facilities, affecting roughly 84,270 people across six districts.

The deluge also devastated hydropower infrastructure, damaging multiple projects and reducing generation capacity by 431 MW — approximately 10% of Nepal’s total output.

An analysis by the Kathmandu-based think tank Change Initiative estimated preliminary losses at between $1.38 and $ 2.70 billion, roughly equivalent to 4% of Nepal’s GDP.

More than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 are still missing from Nepal's recent flash floods [Getty]

A climate funding gap

Experts said the August 2026 Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster was not just a natural shock — it was the predictable outcome of a long-standing climate finance gap.

For years, Nepal’s efforts to adapt to the worst effects of climate change have been constrained by insufficient and fragmented financing, leaving the country without the systems needed to protect people living in the path of glacier- and flood-related hazards.

Nepal has received only about $400 million in total climate finance to date.

But its government estimates it will need roughly $46 billion by 2030 alone to implement its National Adaptation Plan to adapt to the expected effects of climate change, such as floods, landslides, and similar disasters.

This leaves a shortfall of around $45.6 billion, meaning the country’s climate finance needs are more than 100 times what it has received so far.

Furthermore, 61% of the climate finance Nepal receives is in the form of loans, deepening its debt even as climate impacts escalate.

This funding model severely limits support on the ground.

A key $49.9 million project aimed at protecting 2.4 million people in glacial river basins, such as Sarita's community, has only $9.2 million — all of which was disbursed to the UNDP for early-warning and risk-reduction activities.

Global safety nets offer little relief when disasters strike. By July 2026, 119 countries had filed funding requests totalling $2.8 billion with the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), but only $342 million was available for its active pilot phase.

The Fund, established at COP27 in Egypt, has been pledged $822 million by donor nations but has received only $485 million.

The erosion of international support

Alongside the funding gap, vital international support is being rapidly withdrawn.

The SERVIR–Hindu Kush Himalaya initiative, a USAID-funded regional hub that provided critical satellite data and tools for disaster monitoring across the region, was “formally concluded” in January 2025 following a stop-work notice from the United States, despite its contract running till the end of 2026.

A few days after the flood, former USAID official Jeremy Konyndyk noted that DOGE-led actions "killed $420m worth of climate work at NASA" and, in the process, cancelled all seven Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) projects in Nepal — dismantling early warning mechanisms that could have alerted farmers like Pyakurel before the waters rose.

Birendra Bajracharya, former director of the SERVIR-HKH project, told The New Arab that "funding cuts had stalled efforts to improve avalanche situational awareness during heavy rainfall."

"The work to detect slope speeds for avalanche forecasting also could not be completed," he added.

The programme was identifying areas at risk of glacier lake outburst floods so downstream communities could better prepare for potential disasters. Then Donald Trump cut its funding.

Closely watching USAID funding cuts, Dr Ramesh Poudel, Associate Professor in the Central Department of Economics, said that the recent USAID cuts have eroded Nepali trust in America, despite Nepal’s significant contributions of manpower to the United States.

According to him, thousands of Nepalis have worked as security guards, drivers, cooks and base‑support staff for private contractors supporting US operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Nepali doctors, nurses and other health workers are employed in US hospitals and care facilities; many other Nepalis in the United States work in informal and low‑wage sectors.

"Imported development and parasitic consciousness do not always benefit us. We must become self-reliant," he said.

Dr Ramesh warned that when international aid is abruptly halted, existing projects collapse and progress is set back by a decade, because Nepal has historically outsourced its development. Filling the massive funding gaps left by the US withdrawal remains highly unlikely in the near term, he explained.

"Climate finance must fund technology and capacity-building across all three pillars — mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage," Raju Pandit Chhetri, Executive Director of Prakriti Resource Centre, told The New Arab .

"Mitigation avoids or reduces greenhouse gas emissions; adaptation helps communities adjust to a changing climate; and when adaptation is no longer possible, as in the Bhotekoshi flood, the result is loss and damage."

Raju said that the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement oblige developed countries to provide climate finance to developing nations, which have contributed far less to the crisis, face its worst impacts, and have the least capacity to respond.

"From a climate justice perspective, climate finance must therefore flow from developed to developing countries and be implemented effectively," he added.

Uttam Babu Shrestha, director of the Global Institute for Interdisciplinary Studies (GIIS), told The New Arab that developing countries have made climate-finance promises they haven’t kept, and the money they pledged has largely not materialised.

"Even the money that’s available is hard to access, while our needs keep growing dramatically. Because mitigation efforts in developed countries have fallen behind, temperatures are rising, and climate impacts are worsening," he said.

Nepali activists led by Professor Doctor Govinda KC protest against the recent executive order by US President Donald Trump to shut down USAID and cut funding for WHO in Kathmandu, Nepal, on February 18, 2025 [Getty]

'The real solution is to cut carbon emissions;

An Oxfam report from May 2026 showed that developing countries will need about $2.4 trillion per year in climate investment by 2030, rising to roughly $3.2-3.3 trillion per year by 2035 to meet the Paris Agreement and development goals.

Yet adaptation remains severely underfunded, and finance for loss and damage is still largely uncosted and poorly tracked.

Wealthier nations frequently overstate their climate finance contributions by using ambiguous reporting rules and counting loans at full face value.

Many climate finance providers adopt a risk-averse approach.

Consequently, around 90% of climate finance is directed toward middle-income, high-emission countries, leaving lower-income, fragile, and conflict-affected nations with only a fraction of the funding they need.

"The key point is that we’re not looking to the Western world to solve all our problems. Some things can be funded from our own budget and the private sector," Raju said.

Climate analyst Manjeet Dhakal said that the real challenge is staying true to the international climate process, honouring what countries have agreed to and responding to the needs and courage of future generations.

"The real solution is to cut carbon emissions. If we keep emitting carbon, climate disasters will only get worse. Climate finance can help us cope in the short term, but it doesn’t solve the root problem; it just delays it," Manjeet said.

He added that reaching out to the climate finance community isn’t about handing out money to vulnerable communities.

"It’s about enabling them to live with dignity, continue their education, and access rehabilitation and other essential support," he stated.

For people like Sarita Pyakurel, the climate finance debate is not just about figures on a balance sheet — it’s about whether the international system can turn its promises into meaningful support for people like her.

She has felt the effects of disaster more than most.

Nepal’s 2015 earthquake destroyed her home, the 2025 floods wiped away her fields, and this latest deluge carried away what she had left.

"I do not know where to turn," she said.

Sunita Neupane is an independent investigative journalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal. She specialises in high-impact reporting on human rights, public health, and climate justice

title: Tibet-Nepal Mudslide: The shocking cost of climate destruction, imperialism and dictatorship - 社會主義行動
description: Tibet-Nepal Mudslide: The shocking cost of climate destruction, imperialism and dictatorship  社會主義行動
publisher.title: 社會主義行動
full_article:
More than one thousand dead in Nepal – no credible death toll yet reported on the Chinese side

chinaworker.info reporters

The horror of the Himalayan disaster of August 26-27, on the border between Tibet and Nepal, was expressed by one woman who narrowly escaped when the bus she was travelling in was swept away: “It was water mixed with mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us.”

This was one of the most severe natural disasters to strike the Himalayan region in recent years. A massive glacial collapse occurred on the northern slope of Langtang Lirung peak in Nepal, at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres. Ice and underlying bedrock crashed down at high speed, carrying with it mud and debris from the mountainside, creating a colossal mudslide and flash floods that raced down the river valley on the Tibetan side of the border, then striking the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and the Rasuwa district of Nepal. It crashed through the Trishula River valley for 72 kilometres, bringing death and unfathomable destruction. Some of the dead bodies were carried into India, 150 kilometres downstream.

Initially, seismologists mistook the incident for a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. The force of the collapsing rock and ice triggered a 5.2 reading on the Richter scale – equal in power to the Hiroshima atom bomb. Wherever the mudslide passed, villages, roads, bridges and hydroelectric facilities were almost completely levelled. 40 kilometres of road and 19 bridges were swept away. Dozens of settlements and even whole villages were flattened. 2.2 million tonnes of debris was dumped in the disaster zone.

As of 14 September, 1,385 people are reported dead in Nepal, with 5,130 missing. The official toll in China is 43 dead and 519 missing. Several Chinese-built hydroelectric power stations in Nepal were buried, and around 900 workers were at one point unaccounted for, with dozens of them possibly still trapped in underground tunnels.

chinaworker.info express our condolences to all those who have lost their families, homes and livelihoods. However, in the face of such a massive disaster, we cannot simply “unite in grief” but need to look at why, how, and what caused this disaster.

The climate crisis – caused by capitalism’s destruction of the planet’s resources – is making such extreme events even more dangerous. The lack of democratic control by the working class and poor majority, information blackouts, and a so-called development model geared only to capitalist and geopolitical i.e. militarist interests, have further amplified the disaster.

No “negative” news

There is a stark contrast in the transparency of information between China and Nepal, despite the fact that China is far richer than Nepal with an economy 100 times bigger. Nepal has continued to publish figures on the dead, missing, and foreign travellers, whilst seeking relief supplies from foreign governments and NGOs. The Nepalese immigration authorities even utilised electronic records to reconstruct the entry records from the morning of the disaster.

On the Chinese side, however, the familiar apparatus of the CCP’s dictatorial information control was once again set in motion. In the early stages of the disaster, officials reported three deaths and several hundred missing persons; thereafter, updates to the death toll were slow to come.

Surveillance footage released by members of the public which showed the five-storey Gyirong Gate border crossing being completely demolished by the mudslide was deleted within the Great Firewall. For the Chinese dictatorship such images, which convey vulnerability and failure, are not a good fit with Beijing’s “invincible” propaganda. Beijing’s Ministry of Public Security reported that ten people had been detained accused of “spreading false information” online.

Journalists were reportedly barred from entering the disaster area on their own to interview survivors and their families. It was not until nearly two weeks after the disaster that Beijing first arranged for a small number of foreign media outlets to enter the core disaster zone.

The CCP dictatorship routinely bans “negative” news reports, operates in near total secrecy, and downplays numbers of fatalities. It did this on a massive scale during the COVID-19 pandemic. Following the sudden end of China’s ‘zero-COVID’ policy in late 2022, hospitals and crematoria were overwhelmed, yet the authorities temporarily ceased publishing figures on infections and deaths; to this day, the number of lives lost remains a mystery. Such is the logic of authoritarian rule. For the dictatorship, information is first and foremost a tool for maintaining the regime’s image and ‘social stability’, a euphemism for regime control.

How to report on the Himalayan catastrophe is an especially sensitive problem given China’s intensified repressive controls and national oppression in Tibet. In July, Beijing adopted its new ‘ethnic unity law’, which further cements the CCP’s Han chauvinist doctrine. Under this law, promoting minority languages or reporting human rights abuses are further criminalized.

Climate destruction

The Himalayan catastrophe is the latest evidence of a rapidly worsening climate crisis. Coastal provinces of China have been battered by four severe typhoons so far this year. Over 130 people were killed during “historically rare” flooding in Guangxi province. Europe has suffered from months of drought and record-breaking heat in 2026. As ISA’s Arne Johansson explains in his report, ‘Extreme Weather Disasters – The Planet is Fighting Back’, the heatwave will wipe out the entire 1% GDP growth projected in the EU this year.

The Himalayas and surrounding region are sometimes called the “Third Pole” because they contain the biggest volume of glacial ice and snow outside of the north and south poles. Likewise it is among the regions most impacted by climate change, with temperatures warming at twice the global average. China is the world’s biggest source of climate destruction, accounting for one-third of global greenhouse emissions.

This is accelerating the retreat of glaciers on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and in the Himalayas. Since 1980, there has been a marked increase in glacial lake outburst floods in the region, with the China-Nepal border being one of the areas where the risk has risen most significantly over the past decade. A 2023 paper by the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences states that potential glacial lake outbursts now threaten more than 55,000 buildings, 105 hydropower projects, and thousands of kilometres of roads and bridges.

This is by no means the first time that Gyirong has been the subject of warnings. In 2025, floods along the China-Nepal border swept away the Friendship Bridge and left many people missing. Just one year later, an even greater disaster has struck the same region.

Imperialism and geopolitical competition

Meanwhile, the capitalist CCP regime continues to regard the geologically fragile Himalayan region, an area of intense tectonic activity, as a frontline for infrastructure expansion and geopolitical competition. Here, Chinese imperialism vies for regional hegemony and control with aspiring Indian imperialism. The two neighbours engaged in a deadly border conflict in 2020 at Galwan, some 1,000 kilometres to the west of the current disaster zone. Nepal is landlocked between India and China-controlled Tibet.

Since Nepal’s then Maoist-led government in 2017 signed up for China’s imperialist ‘Belt and Road Initiative’, Chinese loans and construction in Nepal have also skyrocketed. Projects include the China-Nepal Highway and the planned China-Nepal railway.

Studies have identified hundreds of potential landslides, some of which directly threaten the highway and planned railway. Road excavation, tunnelling, hydropower and other engineering activities further increases environmental pressures in the region.

This grandiose infrastructure roll out is capitalist and imperialist in nature. It is not undertaken to improve the conditions of the local population or Nepal’s economy, but primarily to further Beijing’s drive for both “clean energy” resources and military-strategic control (to maintain its hold on Tibet). The construction frenzy may have been an additional aggravating factor behind the August disaster, magnifying the impact of climate change. The reengineering and narrowing of natural river valleys and floodplains, using millions of tonnes of concrete, could act as an accelerator and amplifier of the destructive power of floods.

China now accounts for over half of Nepal’s foreign investment. It has funded and built 12 hydropower and dam projects in Nepal – every single one of which was severely damaged or swamped during the August mudslide, according to the BBC.

Democratic working class control

Especially at a time when climate change is rapidly increasing the risks in the volatile Himalayan region, all construction projects must undergo open and democratically-controlled environmental and geological assessments. This demands a system of democratic working class control over the economic and political system, with real independent workers’ organisations and trade unions, a free working class controlled media and full equality and democratic rights for all ethnic groups. This is what real socialism means. These necessary changes are impossible within the cage of tyrannical capitalist rule under the CCP.

There is a need for full transparency regarding the number of deaths, missing persons and border crossing data in the disaster-stricken areas, an end to the media blackout, and unrestricted access for disaster victims, their families, and reporters.

All hydropower, railway, road and mining projects in Tibet and the Himalayan region must undergo geological and environmental safety assessments with veto power in the hands of the working class and local poor. Independent workers’ unions must be legalised and provided full access. High-risk areas require the establishment of transnational glacier monitoring, early warning and evacuation systems, all under democratic public ownership and control instead of prioritising ‘prestige projects’ and military expansion.

The August catastrophe is a sharp warning. In defiance of the scientific evidence and previous promises to reduce emissions and limit temperature increases, capitalists and politicians globally are now prioritising militarism, oil and coal. The struggle against climate disasters is therefore linked to the struggle against the CCP capitalist dictatorship and the global capitalist system.

title: New footage shows devastation of Nepal flood with over 5,000 still missing - Discover SWNS
description: New footage shows devastation of Nepal flood with over 5,000 still missing  Discover SWNS
publisher.title: Discover SWNS
full_article:
Footage from Nepal shows the devastation caused by the deadly landslide and flood that occurred last month – as more than 5,000 people remain missing.

The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).

The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.

Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.

The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

In the most recent statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Nepal on September 11, it was reported that: “13,676 people have been rescued so far, including more than 320 foreign nationals; approximately 5,130 people remain missing, including around 600 foreign nationals from approximately 35 countries; and 1,385 bodies have been recovered from the flood-affected areas.

“These figures remain subject to continuous updating as search, recovery and verification operations continue.”

In the footage, survivors can be seen salvaging whatever they can from the debris, while others stand silently at the places where their homes once stood.

Others are beginning the long process of clearing mud and debris from houses that were destroyed.

Reports say that families are still searching for missing relatives and continue to visit hospitals in Kathmandu, where they look through photographs and lists of missing people displayed on hospital walls.

People are pullied above flood water at Nuwakot, Nepal, September 14 2026.(Pixs via xStringers / SWNS)

The Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) has prepared a report on the extent of the damage caused by the disaster.

The assessment provides an initial picture of the extensive damage and needs arising from the disaster, covering the social, productive and infrastructure sectors as well as cross-cutting areas.

According to the assessment, the total damage caused by the disaster is estimated at approximately $1.8 billion (£1.3 billion), while the estimated loss is approximately $883 million.

The total estimated requirement for reconstruction is approximately $4.78 billion (£3.5 billion).

Of this, approximately $57.67 million (£42.7 million) is estimated to be required for short-term reconstruction and recovery over the next six months, while approximately $4.71 billion (£3.49 billion) is required for longer-term reconstruction.

Men shovel mud from a building in the aftermath of a flood at Nuwakot, Nepal, September 14 2026. (Pixs via xStringers / SWNS)

title: Nearly Three Weeks After Nepal Floods, 70 Americans Remain Unaccounted For - nepyork
description: Nearly Three Weeks After Nepal Floods, 70 Americans Remain Unaccounted For  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
Nearly three weeks after catastrophic flash floods struck Nepal, about 70 Americans remain unaccounted for in the Nepal-China border region, a State Department spokesperson told NepYork on Tuesday. The United States has expanded its response, providing additional forensic assistance, food and logistics support and equipment for search-and-rescue operations as authorities struggle to reach isolated areas.

As of noon Eastern time on Sept. 14, 18 Americans had made their way to safety, according to the State Department. The department cautioned that the figures could change as officials continue efforts to locate, account for and assist U.S. citizens and their families.

“The safety of Americans in the affected area remains our highest priority,” the spokesperson said. “Despite the significant operational challenges, we are using every available means to locate, account for and assist U.S. citizens and their families.”

Forensic Aid to Identify Flood Victims

On Sept. 12, the United States approved an additional $1 million to support Nepal Police in identifying victims of the floods, bringing the total value of U.S. humanitarian, health and forensic assistance following the disaster to more than $5 million, the State Department said.

Photo caption: U.S. officials deliver lifesaving health supplies to the Government of Nepal on Sept. 14 to help restore newborn care, delivery and infection-prevention services at flood-affected health facilities in Rasuwa District. Photo: U.S. Embassy, Nepal.

The new funding, approved through the State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, will provide forensic support to Nepal Police, including DNA analysis kits and other priority supplies needed for disaster victim identification.

FBI forensic specialists are also working with Nepal Police to identify victims and provide specialized disaster victim identification assistance, according to the State Department.

“The conditions responders are operating in within Nepal are extraordinarily difficult,” the spokesperson said. “This disaster destroyed roads, bridges, entire villages, and, in some areas, completely altered the landscape — some previously inhabited places are covered by displaced soil and rocks several feet deep.”

Difficult terrain and damaged infrastructure have slowed search, rescue and relief operations in remote parts of Nepal, particularly near the border with China.

A flood-ravaged village in Nepal. Photo: Pradeep Raj Onta, Nuwakot

Broader U.S. Relief Effort

The new forensic funding is part of a broader U.S. response that includes $3 million in food and logistics assistance through the World Food Program. The funding is expected to provide up to three months of emergency food supplies to 10,000 flood-affected households and help overcome supply-chain barriers through air and ground transportation to isolated communities.

The United States has also provided $685,000 through Catholic Relief Services for food, shelter, water, sanitation, hygiene, protection and cash assistance. The aid includes food and shelter supplies, blankets, plastic sheeting, tents, solar lights and dignity kits. Catholic Relief Services is also operating child-friendly spaces for children affected by the floods, according to the State Department.

Another $365,000 has been allocated for health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene programs through Jhpiego, FHI 360 and UNICEF.

The U.S. military has delivered 5,000 specialized disaster victim recovery supplies, 500 first-aid kits, stretchers and front-end loaders to support Nepal-led search, rescue and recovery operations. A four-member U.S. military civil affairs team is also in Nepal to help address humanitarian needs following the disaster.

A Drone for Remote Flood Zones

In another newly announced measure, the U.S. Embassy in Nepal provided the Armed Police Force with a U.S.-made Freefly Alta X Gen2 commercial cargo drone to help deliver critical supplies to isolated communities affected by the floods.

In a Monday social media post, the U.S. Embassy in Nepal said Deputy Chief of Mission Scott Urbom, Public Affairs Chief Mike Harker and Regional Security Officer Wil Vaughn joined the Armed Police Force, Nepal and Seven Summit Treks for the handover of the drone.

The embassy said the Armed Police Force will use the aircraft to deliver critical supplies to remote, flood-affected communities where difficult terrain limits access.

Photo: U.S. Embassy, Nepal.

Seven Summit Treks had previously tested the drone on Ama Dablam as part of the embassy’s Ascent Summit, successfully carrying oxygen cylinders and mountaineering equipment between high camps under extreme conditions, according to the embassy. The high-altitude test in the Everest region demonstrated a potential use for the technology in some of Nepal’s most difficult terrain.

The drone handover is part of broader U.S. support for Nepal’s flood response, including humanitarian, logistical, forensic, consular and other technical assistance for affected communities and families.

“The United States continues to extend our deepest sympathy to all those affected by the flooding in Nepal and their families,” the State Department said. The department said it would continue coordinating with the Nepal government and local partners as conditions evolve.

“However, this is a rapidly evolving operation, and we are working closely with our local partners on the ground to adapt to conditions as they change,” the spokesperson said.

The United States remains prepared to provide additional assistance based on Nepal’s needs, the State Department said.

The department has posted updates and resources for affected Americans and their families on its Nepal Flash Floods Information webpage.

title: Climate change likely worsened conditions behind Nepal’s deadly mountain collapse - The Climate Watch
description: Climate change likely worsened conditions behind Nepal’s deadly mountain collapse  The Climate Watch
publisher.title: The Climate Watch
full_article:
Scientists say warming has destabilised Himalayan glaciers and frozen ground, while the disaster exposed the limits of Nepal’s existing adaptation and early warning measures.

Climate change contributed to the thinning of glaciers and thawing of frozen ground in the Himalayas, which likely played a role in the deadly rock and ice collapse in Nepal last month, according to a new scientific analysis.

The study was carried out by an international team of glaciologists and climate scientists.

More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a large section of rock and glacier collapsed from Langtang Lirung mountain on August 26. The collapse triggered a huge flow of water, ice and debris that swept through communities downstream.

Scientists said the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event. Instead, it was the result of several geological and climate-related factors coming together.

“Climate warming, caused by humans burning fossil fuels, is melting ice and snow in the Himalayas, reducing glacier coverage and thawing permafrost,” said Professor Bethan Davies, Professor of Glaciology at Newcastle University.

“This is making mountain slopes less stable and increasing the risk of disasters like this one. Urgent action is needed to reduce emissions and prevent faster melting and greater risks in the future,” she said.

According to the study, decades of warming have pushed the freezing line-the level above which temperatures remain below zero degrees Celsius-upward by about 100 metres every decade.

As a result, glaciers are retreating and frozen ground and ice inside cracks in mountain rocks are exposed to warmer temperatures for longer periods. This can weaken the slopes and make them more likely to collapse.

The researchers identified several factors that may have contributed to the collapse. Glacier thinning reduced the ice that helps stabilise mountain slopes, while increased melting may have added more water to the area.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015 may also have weakened the slope before the latest collapse. However, scientists said they cannot yet confirm how much the earthquake contributed to the 2026 disaster.

Manjeet Dhakal, Director of Climate Analytics South Asia, said the disaster was a serious warning about the growing risks faced by people living in a rapidly warming Himalaya.

“Rising temperatures are changing glaciers, snow, permafrost and the wider mountain environment, creating increasingly complex hazards,” Dhakal said.

He said the size of the disaster has tested Nepal’s ability to respond and has shown the limits of existing adaptation measures. He called for faster cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, stronger monitoring and early warning systems, better understanding of mountain risks and greater international climate finance for countries such as Nepal.

Temperatures were also unusually high just before the disaster. July and August 2026 were the warmest on record in the local area, according to the analysis. Heavy snowfall in October and November 2025 also provided additional water that later contributed to melting before the collapse.

The study found that climate change has increased July and August temperatures in the area by about 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with pre-industrial times. Climate change has increased annual temperatures in the region by about 2 degrees Celsius.

However, scientists stressed that the study does not prove that the collapse would not have happened without climate change. Instead, it shows that rising temperatures are changing the Himalayan environment and affecting several factors that can make mountain slopes unstable.

The disaster has also highlighted the limits of adaptation. Nepal has early warning systems and disaster preparedness plans, but the scale and complexity of this event were beyond the capacity of existing measures, the study said.

Professor Friederike Otto of Imperial College London said the study was different from a traditional World Weather Attribution study because it did not examine a single extreme weather event. Instead, scientists looked at a multi-stage mountain disaster involving many factors.

She said the disaster also raised an issue of climate justice, as communities in Nepal are facing the effects of a global crisis largely driven by fossil-fuel emissions.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction,” Otto said. She warned that without faster action to reduce fossil-fuel use, disasters of this scale could become more common in the future.

The researchers are calling for faster reductions in fossil-fuel emissions, stronger monitoring of glaciers and high-altitude permafrost, improved early warning systems and greater investment in understanding mountain hazards.

They also called for increased international climate finance to help vulnerable countries such as Nepal prepare for and recover from the growing risks linked to a warming Himalaya.
